title: Dependency injection: what happens when a singleton depends on a scoped service?
description: Understand DI lifetimes in ASP.NET Core, why a singleton holding a scoped service is problematic, and the correct patterns to resolve it.

data.text: ASP.NET Core's built-in dependency injection container manages three service lifetimes: transient, scoped, and singleton. Interviewers love this question because it tests whether you understand the container's contracts or just memorized definitions.

A singleton lives once for the entire application lifetime. A scoped service lives once per HTTP request (or explicit scope). If a singleton depends on a scoped service, the container faces an impossible choice: should it inject one instance and reuse it across requests, or create a new one for each request?

In ASP.NET Core, the default container throws `InvalidOperationException` at build time or resolve time when a singleton directly depends on a scoped or transient service. The framework prevents you from making the mistake rather than silently producing incorrect behavior.

data.title: Problematic registration
data.content: This code will fail because the container cannot resolve the scoped dependency into the singleton.

data.title: Resolved, not injected
data.text: If you inject an `IServiceProvider` into the singleton and call `GetRequiredService<IOrderRepository>()` inside a request, the container will hand you a scoped instance. That is technically allowed, but you are now hiding a dependency and coupling the singleton to the container's resolve-time behavior.

The right fix depends on intent. If the singleton genuinely needs per-request data, it should not be a singleton. If it only needs the scoped service for a small operation, introduce an abstraction that the singleton can call safely.

data.title: Preferred approaches
items: Change the singleton to scoped or transient if it genuinely needs request-scoped state.
Introduce a factory interface that accepts the scoped dependency as a method parameter.
Inject `IServiceProvider` and resolve the scoped service inside a manually created scope.
Use `IOptions<T>` or configuration objects to pass read-only settings from singleton to scoped code.

data.title: Factory pattern
data.content: The singleton calls a factory method that receives the scoped dependency only when needed, keeping lifetimes clean.

data.text: Interviewers often ask this to see if you think about object lifetimes, thread safety, and testability. A strong answer mentions: why the default container rejects the registration, what happens if you bypass the check with `IServiceProvider`, and how you would redesign the class graph so each layer has a clear responsibility.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: A singleton should never directly own a scoped or transient instance.
The default ASP.NET Core container throws to protect you.
Use factories or redesign boundaries when lifetimes conflict.
Always explain the 'why' behind the lifetime choice in interviews.
data.takeaway: Mismatched lifetimes are a design smell: fix the class graph, not just the registration.
